title: Why The Earliest Writing Was Bookkeeping
text:
Writing was not invented to record poetry, laws, or the deeds of kings. In southern Mesopotamia, the earliest tablets we can read are inventories: quantities of barley, numbers of sheep, rations issued to workers. That origin explains a great deal about how the system developed. Before tablets, accountants used small clay tokens of different shapes, sealed inside clay envelopes, to record transactions. Because a sealed envelope hid its own contents, scribes began pressing the tokens into the outer surface before enclosing them. Eventually somebody realised the impressions alone would do, and the envelope became a tablet.

At that stage the marks were still pictures of things, tied closely to the commodity being counted. The decisive step came when signs began to stand for sounds rather than objects. A sign for one word could now be borrowed for any word that sounded similar, which meant personal names, grammatical endings and abstract ideas could all be written down. Only then does the record widen to include letters, hymns, legal cases and school exercises. The administrative purpose came first; literature arrived centuries later, as a by-product of a tool built for bookkeeping.
points: The earliest readable Mesopotamian tablets are administrative records of grain, animals and rations.
Before tablets, accountants recorded transactions with clay tokens sealed inside clay envelopes.
Scribes pressed the tokens onto the envelope's surface, and eventually the impressions replaced the envelope.
Early signs were pictures tied to the goods being counted.
The decisive change was signs standing for sounds, which allowed names, grammar and abstract ideas.
Literature and law appear only later; the system began as a bookkeeping tool.
